record.paper_title: Unsolved Problems in Ordered and Orderable Groups
record.original_question: Let G be an orderable group such that every order on every subgroup of G is central. Is every right order on G a Conrad right order?

evidence.quote: 2.28. (V. V. Bludov, A. H. Rhemtulla) Let G be an orderable group such that every order on every subgroup of G is central. Is every right order on G a Conrad right order?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. A group $G$ is called orderable (two-sided orderable) if there exists a total order $\leq$ on $G$ that is invariant under both left and right multiplication: for all $a,b,x,y\in G$, $a\leq b$ implies $xay\leq xby$. A right order on $G$ is a total order $\leq$ such that $a\leq b$ implies $ax\leq bx$ for all $x\in G$. Equivalently, a right order is determined by its positive cone $P=\{g\in G : g>1\}$, which satisfies $P\cdot P\subseteq P$, $P\cap P^{-1}=\emptyset$, and $P\cup P^{-1}\cup\{1\}=G$.

A two-sided order on a subgroup $H\leq G$ is called central if its positive cone is closed under conjugation by every element of $H$ (equivalently, the order is invariant under inner automorphisms of $H$); for two-sided orders this is automatic, so the condition is meaningful when applied uniformly to all subgroups: every two-sided order on every subgroup $H\leq G$ has its positive cone normal in $H$.

A right order $\leq$ on $G$ with positive cone $P$ is called a Conrad right order (or satisfies the Conrad property) if for every $a,b\in P$ there is a positive integer $n$ such that $a^n b > a$, equivalently, every finitely generated subgroup of $G$ has a nontrivial order-convex normal subgroup with infinite cyclic quotient under the induced order.

Question. Let $G$ be an orderable group such that every two-sided order on every subgroup of $G$ is central. Must every right order on $G$ be a Conrad right order?
